references.text: The same expression, "so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth," is used again during the plague of hail and emphasizes the Lord's unique power.
Moses reminds Israel that they saw the Lord's works "so that you may know that the Lord is God; there is no other besides him."
It confirms that "the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other," reflecting the theme of the Lord's uniqueness.
The Lord declares, "I am the Lord; there is no other; besides me there is no god," confirming the same theme of God's unique nature.
God declares, "I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me," echoing Moses' words to Pharaoh.
Both verses focus on affirming God's existence and authority before skeptics (the people/Pharaoh) through coming signs.
A direct parallel in the same plague where "tomorrow" is used as the timeframe for a sign intended to convince Pharaoh of God's power.
A theological parallel where miracles (flies/thunder) are used specifically so that Pharaoh may "know" or "be aware" of God's supremacy.
